strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: extracting nested low-rank submodels from a single pretrained model for adaptive deployment under varying budgets.

Provides a theoretical analysis in a simplified linear setting that explains why post-training selection and all-submodel learning can fail, and why nested subspace learning can recover the Pareto front; the theory is supported by controlled simulations.
Proposes a principled three-stage framework combining activation-aware DataSVD initialization, dynamic-programming-based rank allocation, and knowledge-distillation refinement.
Empirically evaluates the method on a broad set of models and modalities, including GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B/8B, and DINOv3 ViTs, with comparisons to SVD/DataSVD+DP and ACIP.
Includes useful ablations on calibration sample size, independent layer training, and the importance of joint submodel training.
Provides an honest limitations section and appropriate impact statement.
Introduces a practical inference-time reparameterization that can reduce the cost of low-rank matrix-vector multiplication.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results are for a single linear matrix and do not directly establish the claimed Pareto-optimal behavior in deep nonlinear networks; the method relies on strong, largely unvalidated assumptions such as additivity of layer-wise errors and preservation of the initial importance ordering after training.
The paper overclaims that FlexRank 'recovers the true Pareto front in DNNs' based on a small four-layer MNIST experiment, which is not sufficient evidence for large-scale LLM or ViT settings.

The dynamic-programming rank-selection procedure is underspecified: the manuscript does not give the recurrence, state space, how the sensitivity matrix is converted into additive errors, or how nestedness is enforced during DP. This limits reproducibility of the core algorithmic contribution.

Evaluation uses parameter count as a proxy for deployment cost; no actual FLOPs, latency, memory footprint, or hardware measurements are reported, despite the paper's framing around adaptive deployment and efficiency-performance trade-offs.

The comparison with ACIP appears potentially unfair: the main figure shows 'ACIP (w/o LoRA)', while FlexRank uses distillation; the full ACIP with LoRA repair is not consistently compared. Other low-rank methods (e.g., SVD-LLM, DRONE, ASVD, A3) and flexible-network methods (e.g., MatFormer, Flextron, LLamaflex) are mentioned but not experimentally compared.
Post-adaptation results in Table 1 show severe degradation at reduced budgets (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B code drops from 33.76 at 1× to 6.67 at 0.6×), which contradicts the claim of graceful degradation.
There is no ablation isolating the benefit of DP-based mask selection versus uniform, random, or heuristic nested masks under the same training budget, so the source of the reported gains is unclear.
The ASL proof's claim that the zero set is a proper linear subspace is questionable because λ depends nonlinearly on σ through soft-thresholding; the proof glosses over this technical issue.

Main results in Figures 4 and 5 lack exact numerical tables, confidence intervals, and clear baseline definitions, making it difficult to assess the magnitude and statistical significance of the improvements.
The method still requires substantial training compute (e.g., 8 nodes for 6 days for Llama-3.1-8B), which may limit the practical 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' promise.

Some claims, such as being the 'first work' to design flexible models at scale in factorized space and 'outperforming state-of-the-art compression and elasticity approaches', are overstated relative to the experiments presented.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (elastic deployment across heterogeneous cost budgets) and proposes a coherent three-stage pipeline—data-aware SVD initialization, a dynamic-programming global rank ordering, and nested-submodel distillation—that is clearly described and illustrated (Fig. 1).

Section 4 provides a useful conceptual framing (PTS / ASL / NSL) for why post-hoc selection and all-subspace learning can fail and why nestedness matters, which is an interesting lens even if restricted to linear/matrix settings.

The empirical scope is broad: GPT-2, three Llama models (1B/3B/8B), and DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B, covering both NLP (lm-eval-harness commonsense) and CV (ImageNet1K) tasks, plus a post-adaptation LoRA study (Table 1).
The inference-cost observation in Sec. 3.5 (absorbing a gauge transform G to reduce U-multiplication cost) and the comparative summary in Table 2 are helpful practical additions.
An honest limitations discussion (Sec. 7, Sec. D.4) is provided, including the compute constraints.
weaknesses: Theory–method gap: Theorems 4.1–4.3 concern a single linear layer / matrix factorization, yet the paper repeatedly uses them to justify behavior on deep nonlinear networks. The 'interference' mechanism behind ASL failure is only demonstrated on a synthetic 10-dim setup and a 2x2 construction (Cor. B.8), so the theory does not rigorously support the central claim about deep models.

Thm 4.3 is close to tautological: given Eckart–Young and the construction, the proof assumes all per-rank lower bounds are simultaneously achievable—which is precisely the property being claimed—so 'NSL recovers the Pareto front' is largely asserted rather than derived for the general case.

The key approximation (that the layer-wise importance ordering identified from θ0 is preserved after training) is validated only on a 4-layer MNIST network (Sec. 3.4, Fig. 3). For LLMs and ViTs the ordering is simply assumed, so the paper's 'recovering the true Pareto front' claim does not transfer to the scales actually evaluated.

The DP search relies on (i) approximate additivity of per-layer errors and (ii) layer probing that perturbs one layer at a time. Both ignore cross-layer interactions; the paper acknowledges this but provides no quantification of how much this heuristic degrades the resulting ordering.

Confounded comparisons: FlexRank (with distillation) is compared mainly against SVD/DataSVD without training and against ACIP run without LoRA—a version the authors themselves characterize as a PTS algorithm. This does not isolate the effect of nested training and does not fairly compare against strong trained low-rank baselines that are discussed but not run (SVD-LLM, ASVD, A3, DRONE).

Despite the 'adaptive deployment across cost budgets' framing, cost is measured only as parameter count; there are no wall-clock latency, memory, or throughput measurements, so the deployment/efficiency claims are unsupported empirically.

Reproducibility is limited: training requires 2–8 A100 nodes for 2–6 days per model, main-text results lack seeds/error bars, and many essential details (search, hyperparameters, evaluation) are deferred to the appendix.

Limited methodological novelty: data-aware SVD, nested/slimmable submodels, and distillation are all established components; the novel element is mainly their combination plus a heuristic DP ordering, and the paper itself notes DataSVD has prior art.

strengths: The theoretical analysis in Sec. 4 is a genuine contribution: it formalizes why Post-Training Selection (Thm. 4.1) and All-Subspaces Learning (Thm. 4.2) cannot recover the Pareto front, and proves that Nested Subspace Learning does (Thm. 4.3). This gives principled justification for the design rather than relying on heuristics, and the controlled experiments in Figs. 2-3 corroborate the theory.

The core method is clean and well-motivated: layer-wise DataSVD for importance ordering, a DP/MCKP formulation for globally optimal nested rank selection with complexity linear in layers and budgets, and distillation-based refinement. The 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' framing is practically relevant.

Empirical breadth is strong, covering GPT-2, three Llama models (1B/3B/8B), and DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B, with both commonsense zero-shot accuracy and post-adaptation (LoRA on math/code) results. The comparison to ACIP and SVD/DataSVD baselines isolates the effect of nested training.

The ablations are informative: Fig. 6 (non-uniform compression profiles), Fig. 7(a) (activation sample-size saturation), Fig. 7(b) (need for end-to-end rather than per-layer training), and Fig. 8 (joint vs. independent submodel training) each target a specific design decision.

The efficient low-rank inference trick (absorbing a gauge G to reduce inference cost to O((m+n-r)r)) is a nice practical addition, and the Sec. 3.4 controlled study showing recovery of the true Pareto front is a compelling validation.
Limitations are discussed honestly (Sec. 7), and the tabular comparison (Tab. 2) clarifies positioning against prior low-rank methods.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are established only for a single linear layer with strict assumptions (distinct singular values, access to the exact optimal selection indices S_r via exhaustive search, gradient descent reaching a global minimizer). The paper acknowledges the additivity assumption for the DP is strong, but provides no formal or quantitative bound on how much this single-layer analysis transfers to deep nonlinear networks; the bridge is empirical only.

DataSVD is essentially the activation-informed decomposition of prior work (Chen et al., 2021), and the paper concedes it 'serves only as initialization.' The genuinely novel components are the nested DP selection and the theory; the incremental novelty should be framed more carefully.

The training regime is limited (~10,000 steps, roughly half an epoch), and full-budget performance does not always match the base model (visible gaps in Fig. 4). This makes it hard to judge whether FlexRank's advantage persists under longer, better-tuned training, and the claim of recovering the Pareto front is based on a small 4-layer MNIST-scale network.

Several methodological details are under-specified: how the nestedness constraint is enforced during DP traversal, how the fixed masks from a proxy θ⁰ interact with the distillation objective, and how budgets map to concrete rank configurations are described only at a high level (Sec. C.2). This limits reproducibility.
Table 1 reports post-adaptation results only for FlexRank submodels with no baseline comparison, so the claim of 'graceful degradation' is not benchmarked against alternatives.

Some empirical results are presented only as figures without accompanying numeric tables (e.g., Figs. 4-5, 8), and per-budget accuracies are not tabulated, making it difficult to assess statistical reliability of the reported gains.

The strong claim that FlexRank 'recovers the true Pareto front' (Sec. 3.4) rests on a single synthetic/controlled experiment; generalization of this optimality claim to the LLM/ViT scale is not demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: elastic deployment of large pretrained models via nested low-rank decomposition, enabling one set of shared weights to produce submodels across budgets.

Provides theoretical insight in a linear setting (Sec. 4): Theorem 4.1 shows post-training selection almost never recovers rank-truncated optima; Theorem 4.2 shows all-subspace learning has a positive optimality gap; Theorem 4.3 shows nested subspace learning recovers the Pareto front. Proofs are provided in App. B.
The proposed pipeline is coherent: DataSVD layer-wise initialization, DP-based rank selection under an additive probe, nested knowledge distillation, and GAR reparameterization for inference savings.
Evaluation is broad: GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, and DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B; compared against SVD, DataSVD, ACIP, LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip, and an independently trained submodel baseline.
Ablations examine activation sample size for DataSVD, independent vs. end-to-end submodel training, and sampling of nested profiles, supporting key design choices.
Limitations are discussed explicitly, including training overhead, lack of adaptive routing evaluation, and inference efficiency considerations.
weaknesses: The formal theory is limited to a linear model without nonlinearities and assumes exact global minimizers; it does not directly guarantee Pareto recovery in deep nonlinear networks, where the method is evaluated.

The DP selection relies on an additivity/ranking-preservation assumption for layer-wise errors; validation is only on small controlled settings (App. C.3, e.g., 10^4 submodels), not on the large LLM/ViT experiments.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release; calibration set size for DP probing is not clearly specified; App. C.3 and D.1 appear inconsistent about whether the controlled setting is synthetic linear data or MNIST.

GAR assumes the top r×r block U_{1:r,:} is invertible, which is not guaranteed; no fallback (e.g., selecting an invertible r×r submatrix and propagating a row permutation) is discussed, potentially affecting deployment.
Main LM/ViT results are shown only as curves in Figs. 4-5 without exact numbers, confidence intervals, or detailed per-task tables, making it harder to assess statistical reliability.

Training overhead is significant: full-rank factors roughly double memory and slow training, and inference speedups are measured only for isolated matrix multiplication (Fig. 10), not end-to-end latency with attention/KV cache.

The claim of recovering the 'true Pareto front' is demonstrated only in small synthetic/MNIST-like settings; for LLMs and ViTs the evidence is empirical and does not establish exact Pareto optimality.

strengths: Provides a clear theoretical analysis for linear models showing that post-training selection (PTS) and all-subspace learning (ASL) fail to recover the Pareto front, while nested subspace learning (NSL) succeeds. Theorems 4.1–4.3 give useful intuition for why nested training is beneficial.

Proposes a practical method (FlexRank) that combines DataSVD initialization, dynamic programming for rank selection, and knowledge distillation of nested submodels. The method is simple to implement and scales to large models.

Introduces Gauge-Aligned Reparametrization (GAR), a clever inference-time trick that reduces the cost of low-rank matrix-vector multiplication to O((m+n-r)r) and is applied uniformly to all rank-based baselines for fair comparison.

Empirical results on LLMs (GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B/8B) and ViTs (DINOv3 up to 7B) show that FlexRank improves accuracy–cost trade-offs over SVD, DataSVD, ACIP, and independently trained submodels. Notably, it outperforms ACIP, a state-of-the-art low-rank elastic method.

Includes thorough ablations: effect of activation sample size, independent layer training vs. end-to-end, importance of submodel sampling, and analysis of the ranking-preservation assumption on a small MNIST network (Spearman 0.991, 94.1% DP success).
weaknesses: The theoretical results are limited to a single linear layer with no activations. The extension to deep nonlinear networks is heuristic and relies on the critical assumption that the relative ordering of submodels from a frozen DataSVD initialization is preserved after training. This assumption is validated only on a tiny MNIST network, not on the large models used in the main experiments.

The dynamic programming rank selection assumes additive errors across layers, which ignores cross-layer interactions. The paper acknowledges this as a strong assumption but only validates it on a small synthetic setting. For deep transformers, no evidence is provided that the additive probe induces a reliable ordering.

Overstated novelty: the paper claims to be 'the first work to lay the theoretical foundation for nested submodel training,' but prior work on nested dropout (Rippel et al., ICML 2014) already studied nested submodel training with theoretical analysis. The paper does not cite or discuss this closely related line of work, undermining the originality claim.

Reproducibility is weakened by the lack of compute details (e.g., GPU hours, hardware used) and an incomplete description of how the training budgets are selected from the Pareto front (the SELECTPROFILES procedure is not fully specified).
Main results (e.g., Fig. 4 and Fig. 5) appear to be single runs without error bars, making it difficult to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements.

Post-adaptation results (Table 1) show severe degradation on code tasks at 0.4× (1.22% for Llama-3.2-1B), which is not 'graceful' and suggests that the submodels lose essential capabilities for some domains.

The paper does not compare against other prominent elastic methods such as Flextron, LLamaflex, or MatFormer, arguing they are orthogonal. However, a direct comparison would strengthen the claims of state-of-the-art performance.
Presentation issues: some figures (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 3) are too small to read, and there are notation inconsistencies (e.g., in Eq. 60, Δθ_l = (Δθ_l - U_l V_l^T) should be (θ_l - U_l V_l^T)).

strengths: The paper proposes a coherent and practical framework, FLEXRANK, for elastic model deployment via nested low-rank decomposition, dynamic-programming rank selection, and knowledge consolidation, enabling a train-once/deploy-everywhere workflow.

The theoretical analysis in the linear setting is a clear contribution: it shows why post-training selection and all-submodel learning fail to recover the Pareto front, and why nested submodel learning can recover it. This gives principled motivation for the method's nestedness constraint.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant, spanning GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, and DINOv3 ViTs up to 7B. Across these settings, FLEXRANK generally improves accuracy-cost trade-offs over SVD/DataSVD/ACIP and remains competitive with LLM-PRUNER and LAYERSKIP.

The GAR reparametrization is a simple but useful inference-time contribution, reducing rank-r matrix-vector cost to O((m+n-r)r) without storing or multiplying a dense r×r block, and it is applied consistently to baselines.

The ablation studies are informative, including analysis of per-module compression profiles, the effect of DataSVD calibration size, the need for end-to-end submodel training, and the importance of nested submodel sampling.
The limitations discussion is honest and covers optimization/adaptivity, training efficiency, and inference efficiency, which is appropriate for a deployment-oriented compression method.
The paper treats research ethics lightly but appropriately; there are no apparent ethical concerns beyond general deployment considerations.
weaknesses: The central DP/additivity and ranking-preservation assumption is only validated in a small 4-layer MNIST setting with 10^4 submodels. Since this assumption drives the global rank allocation, its lack of validation on LLM/ViT-scale models is a significant limitation.

The theoretical guarantees are derived for linear models and do not directly apply to nonlinear transformers. The paper is careful to state this, but the main method still relies on those insights for nonlinear architectures without comparable formal or large-scale empirical validation of the selection assumptions.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no code or artifact release is mentioned, and although datasets and hyperparameters are described, training an 8B model on 5B tokens is expensive and exact replication would be difficult. Some baseline training-budget details also remain ambiguous.

GAR requires the first r rows of U to be invertible, but the paper does not discuss numerical conditioning, rank deficiency, or fallback strategies. This could limit its reliability in practice for arbitrary trained factorizations.

The presentation has several typos and formatting issues (e.g., “1m-eval-harness”, “Grattafori”, “Geeedy”, missing parenthesis in the Algorithm 2 caption, inconsistent FLEXRANK/FlexRank), which reduce polish and clarity.

The comparison claims at “matched training budget” are somewhat ambiguous because different methods use different adaptation/training regimes; the ACIP with/without LoRA comparison may not be fully apples-to-apples.

The claim of being the first to lay a theoretical foundation for nested submodel training and to obtain flexible models at scale may be overstated given prior and concurrent work on nested/elastic architectures (e.g., MatFormer, OFA, Flextron, Llamaflex, and concurrent rank-based elasticity work).
